items.note: Garuḍa engraved as the emblem of the Paramāra dynasty, common to all grants of the house.
Garuḍa image enshrined in a miniature shrine with pillars, three-slab roof and spire, as in vogue in Mālava at that time.
Alphabet is Nāgarī, closely resembling the Māndhātā grant of V.S. 1317.
Record in Sanskrit, 72 stanzas in ornate, highly flown style, generally correct language.
Records endowments of land to Brāhmaṇas at Māndhāta by Anayasiṃha with approval of Jayasiṃhadēva, lord of Dhārā, on 10 August 1274 A.C. (V.S. 1331).
Legend of the origin of the Paramāras as in the Udaipur praśasti: Vasishtha creates a hero named Paramāra; eight descendants named.
Editor takes six of the early names as unhistorical, a creation of the poet's mind: evidence versus tradition.

items.note: Sindhurāja, poet and warrior, brother of Vākpatirāja-Muñja, succeeded by his son Bhōjadeva.
Editor finds the Muñja/Vākpati account confused: the composer does not know they are one king.
Successors listed: Udayāditya's son Naravarman, then Yaśōvarman, Ajayavarman, Vindhyavarman, Subhaṭavarman.
Dēvapāla said to have cut down the lord of the Mlechchhas near Bhillasvāmipura (Bhilsā/Vidishā); read as recapture after Iltutmish's invasion of 1233-34, held by Paramāras for about half a century.
Dēvapāla succeeded by his son Jaitugidēva, then Jayavarman, also known as Jayasiniha.
Verse 52: Jayasiniha both dauhitra and pautra; taken to suggest Dēvapāla succeeded Arjunavarman as son-in-law, bearing on the controversy over his accession.
Footnote: Yādava-Paramāra struggle began in the last quarter of the tenth century, Bhillama II assisting Tailapa against Muñja (Saingamēr grant of 1000 A.C.).
Verse 55: Jayavarman erected temples with golden jars, donated cities, gold and cows to Brāhmaṇas, planted gardens and excavated tanks; particulars not given.
Anayasimha built Śiva temples at Dēvapālapura and Māndhātā and an Ambikā temple at Śākapura, and excavated a tank at Maṇḍapa-durga.
Anayasimha donated a Brahmapurī with wall and street, sixteen temples with golden jars, a guest-house and a stepped well.
Four villages divided into sixteen shares, fourteen to Brāhmaṇas and two kept by the donor.
Record composed by Śrīkaṇṭha, member of Jayavarman's assembly and Trivēdin by heritage, and engraved by Kānhāka.
